abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel coalgebraic framework that fundamentally reconceptualizes the semantics of recursive programs within an enriched category-theoretic setting. Traditional operational and denotational semantics have long been established as complementary perspectives, yet their formal reconciliation has remained elusive. We propose a universal coalgebraic theory that simultaneously captures both semantic approaches through a unified adjunction between the category of behaviour functors and the category of final coalgebras. Our central contribution is the demonstration that greatest fixed-point semantics and least fixed-point semantics arise as dual instances of a single categorical greatest fixed-point operator, thereby establishing a new paradigm for understanding recursion across programming language paradigms. The framework naturally accommodates non-well-founded data structures and provides a principled account of bisimulation as a canonical equivalence relation. By leveraging the duality between algebra and coalgebra, we obtain a mathematical structure that subsumes existing semantic accounts while opening new directions for program verification. This work establishes a foundation for a categorical theory of programs that treats syntax and semantics as equally fundamental aspects of a cohesive mathematical reality.

We present significant theoretical advances in the algebraic semantics of higher-order typed lambda calculi by developing a novel categorical model that overcomes limitations of existing Cartesian closed categories. Traditional domain-theoretic models suffer from restrictive continuity requirements that prevent the direct representation of certain programming language features. Our approach introduces a new class of categories called 'stable reflexive domains' that provide a refined mathematical structure capturing both sequential and parallel computation aspects. We establish a full abstraction result for a polymorphic lambda calculus with sum types and recursive types, significantly improving upon previous partial characterizations. The categorical construction combines elements of domain theory with modern synthetic category theory, yielding a framework where computational behaviour can be characterized through universal properties. Key technical contributions include a new proof of the adequacy of our semantics with respect to contextual equivalence, along with an explicit characterization of the observational preorder in categorical terms. The resulting theory provides not only better mathematical understanding but also practical insights for programming language implementation and verification.

We introduce ProTeCS (Proof Theory Engine for Categorical Systems), a novel interactive theorem proving system based on a foundational theory of categorical logic. Unlike traditional proof assistants that rely on set-theoretic foundations or dependent type theory, ProTeCS implements a genuinely categorical logical framework where judgment forms are represented as morphisms in a slice category. The system supports reasoning across multiple syntactic categories simultaneously, enabling direct formalization of concepts that require translation between different logical settings. A central innovation is the categorical treatment of proof equality, where conversion rules are expressed as natural transformations between functorial proof interpretations. ProTeCS provides a modular architecture for adding new logical theories as categories with specified properties, along with a graphical interface that visualizes categorical constructions. The system includes an automated tactic engine for reasoning with universal properties and adjunctions. We demonstrate ProTeCS through extended case studies in process algebra and programming language semantics, showing how the categorical perspective naturally accommodates complex interoperability scenarios that are awkward in conventional systems.

We describe CCS^D, an extended version of Calculus of Communicating Systems with integrated domain-theoretic verification capabilities. The standard process algebra approach to concurrent system verification suffers from the well-known state explosion problem when attempting to model checking via labelled transition systems. Our system addresses this challenge by incorporating symbolic representation of process behaviour using approximants from domain theory, enabling compositional verification of infinite-state systems. The mathematical foundations rest on establishing that strong and weak bisimulation equivalences can be characterized as greatest fixed points of monotone operators on the complete lattice of process approximations. CCS^D provides a rich specification language combining process algebraic expressions with domain-theoretic recursion schemes, along with a toolchain that generates verification conditions automatically. The system implements an improved version of the local model checking algorithm that exploits the compactness properties of continuous domains to achieve significant efficiency gains. Experimental evaluation on benchmark systems from distributed algorithms literature demonstrates order-of-magnitude improvements in verification time compared to existing tools while maintaining soundness guarantees.
